note: Vol. I No. 43. A DIMENSIONED WAREHOUSE AND ITS WHARF: John T. Temple lets a three-storey store house 40 by 60 feet with a wharf attached of 60 feet front, and a small dwelling house of two rooms, on 20 September 1834. That one notice carries more measured building evidence than the rest of the month together. Beside it a marriage, a death with a New Hampshire origin, a dissolution that exercises ruling 3's veto, two priced estrays, and J. K. Botsford's corner of Dearborn and Lake set in capitals.

claims.notes: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CLAIM IN THE SEPTEMBER RUN, AND IT IS DIMENSIONED. A three-storey store house measuring 40 BY 60 FEET, with a WHARF ATTACHED OF 60 FEET FRONT, on or about South Water Street, to let on 20 September 1834. Every part of that is something this project normally has to infer: a storey count, a footprint in feet, and a wharf whose frontage is given as a number rather than as 'a wharf'. Sixty feet of wharf against a sixty-foot building face means the wharf ran the full width of the lot — river frontage and building frontage are the same measurement — which is the pattern the reconstruction's river margin assumes and has never been able to cite. The same notice lets a SMALL DWELLING HOUSE OF TWO ROOMS, which is the other end of the town's building stock and equally undocumented. PLACEMENT IS `street_only` AND DELIBERATELY SO: 'on South Water-st.' sits at the end of a list of three properties and may govern one of them or all three, and a three-storey warehouse with a wharf cannot stand on the street's south side. Nothing is placed from this until that ambiguity is resolved; what is recorded is the dimensions, which do not depend on it. Compare 1834-09-10 claim c007, where the same man lets two new four-room dwelling houses — Temple is the largest builder the September run names.

claims.notes: A named household with an origin: Thomas and Sarah Hoit, of Stafford county, New Hampshire, resident in Chicago, she dying at forty-two on 16 September 1834 leaving children. The reconstruction's inferred households take their family bands from aggregate figures (T-0272 to T-0274 carry that complaint); this is a real Chicago family with a name, a former county and a size implied by 'a mother'. The eulogy is unsigned but marked 'Com.' — communicated, i.e. supplied by a friend rather than written by the editor.

claims.notes: THE COUNTY'S SOUTHERN BOUNDARY, DRAWN BY LANDMARKS AND NOT BY SURVEY LINES: south of the south side of the Oak Woods, south of a line from thence to Laughton's, south and south west of the Dupage river. Laughton's is a named trading house on the Des Plaines and the Oak Woods a named grove; the militia geography is the town's own mental map of its hinterland, and it is drawn entirely in features rather than sections. The northern battalion's boundary is at 1834-09-03 claim c006 and the two together describe the whole county as its own officers saw it.

claims.notes: AN ESTRAY NOTICE IS A PRICED DESCRIPTION OF A HORSE, and this project has to draw horses. Fifteen hands, eight years, light bay, left hind foot white, saddle marks, a scar on the rump, appraised at fifty dollars; and an iron gray mare of fourteen to fifteen hands, three years, a star on her forehead, at forty-five. Height, colour, markings and value, sworn before a justice. Whatever else these notices are for, they are the best physical description of ordinary 1834 Illinois stock the corpus carries. LaSalle county and not Cook, so nothing is placed.

claims.notes: A second estray, and the price is the point: a five-year-old bay gelding of fifteen hands appraised at twenty-seven dollars and fifty cents against the fifty-dollar bay of claim c010. Two horses of the same height, three weeks apart, before neighbouring justices, at nearly double the price — so appraisal was reading condition and training, not size. Anyone costing draught animals into a 1835 street scene now has three sworn valuations to work from.

claims.notes: A CORNER, SET IN CAPITALS AS THE ADVERTISEMENT'S OWN HEADING: Dearborn and Lake. The corpus already carries Botsford at a Dearborn Street corner; this printing states the cross street outright and dates his commencement to 22 April 1834, so the frontage is occupied for the whole fifteen months before the scene date. Corner placements are the only class that can put a building on a specific ground square without further evidence, and this is one of four in the whole September run.

claims.notes: THE DEMOCRAT'S JOB PRESS, SELLING LEGAL BLANKS TO THE COUNTY'S JUSTICES. The corpus carries the Chicago American's printing office as a business and has not carried the Democrat's; it is entered here from the paper's own advertisement, which is the only kind of evidence a newspaper's job department leaves. It also fixes what the office DID besides print a weekly — the estray notices, attachment writs and probate notices filling these columns all began as blanks bought at this counter.

claims.notes: THE SAME CONSIGNMENT AS 1834-09-10 CLAIM C006, READ DIFFERENTLY. This printing gives 60 sides of sole leather, 130 pairs of boots, 90 of shoes and 45 rifles; the earlier one gives 190 boots and 46 rifles. Same copy date, same advertisement, two OCR readings that disagree on three numerals — which is exactly the reason a quantity out of this batch is not a measurement until two printings agree, and both are recorded so a later pass can see the disagreement instead of inheriting one side of it.
